query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post-deposition heat treatment in an oxidizing atmosphere promotes the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale on FeNiCrCoCu thin film coatings, which in turn governs the overall high-temperature wear resistance by reducing direct metal-to-metal contact, lowering the friction coefficient and wear rate under sliding conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin film protective coating on a conventional metal substrate, produced at room temperature with typical high-entropy alloy microstructure.
generation.intervention: Perform a post-deposition heat treatment in ambient air at 700°C for 1 hour.
generation.conditions: Reciprocating wear tests conducted at elevated temperatures, specifically within the 650°C to 900°C range, under moderate to high normal loads representative of high-temperature industrial applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous and dense oxide layer composed of mixed oxides (e.g., Fe-, Ni-, Cr-, Co-, and Cu-oxides) on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the heat treatment enhances oxidation kinetics at the surface of the FeNiCrCoCu coating, leading to the development of a protective oxide film that prevents direct metallic contact, reduces adhesive and abrasive wear, and lowers the friction coefficient during sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, the heat-treated coatings will exhibit a significantly lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate compared to as-deposited (untreated) coatings; surface analyses (e.g., SEM and XPS) will reveal a continuous, adherent oxide scale on the treated samples.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coatings without any post-deposition heat treatment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable within the temperature range of 650°C to 900°C under reciprocating wear loads typical for high-temperature applications. Its efficacy under significantly lower or higher loads or temperatures remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: The precise composition, thickness, and long-term stability of the protective oxide scale are not fully quantified and could vary with slight changes in processing conditions; furthermore, the optimization of treatment duration and temperature may be needed for maximal benefit.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin film coatings on identical conventional metal substrates. Subject one set to a post-deposition heat treatment in air at 700°C for 1 hour, while keeping the other set as-deposited as a control. Then, perform reciprocating wear tests at 800°C under identical load conditions. Use surface analytical techniques such as scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to characterize the presence and morphology of the oxide scale on both sets.
measurements: Continuity, composition, and thickness of the surface oxide layer (via SEM/XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated coatings do not form a continuous, adherent oxide layer, or if their friction coefficient and wear rate are not significantly lower than those of the as-deposited coatings, then the hypothesis that the protective oxide film governs the high-temperature wear resistance would be falsified.

Microstructural Evolution of AlCoCrFeNiSi High-Entropy Alloy Powder during Mechanical Alloying and Its Coating Performance

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising structural materials due to their excellent comprehensive performances. The use of mechanically alloyed powders to deposit HEA coatings through atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) is an effective approach that can broaden the application areas of the HEAs. In this paper, a ductility–brittleness AlCoCrFeNiSi system was chosen as an object of study, and the detailed evolution of the surface morphology, particle size distribution, and microstructure of the powder during mechanical alloying was investigated. An AlCoCrFeNiSi HEA coating was deposited using powder milled for 10 h, which can be used as an ideal feedstock for APS. The surface morphology, microstructure, microhardness, and wear behavior of the coating at room temperature were investigated. The results showed that as the milling time increased, the particle size first increased, and then decreased. Studying the Effect of Cold Rolling and Heat Treatment on the Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of the Fe36Mn20Ni20Cr16Al5Si3 High Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractIn this study, a multi-component FeMnNiCrAlSi high-entropy alloy, chosen through Thermo-Calc® software (2021a, Stockholm, Sweden) calculation and produced by electric arc melting, was studied for phase continents and mechanical properties. The results elucidated that the cold rolled condition (area reduction ratio about 86%) was in the form of elongated grains with a dendritic structure. Also, small amounts of the BCC phase were precipitated at the grain boundaries. The annealed sample shows features of BCC phase and different sizes of intermetallics. These results coincided with the predictions of Thermo-Calc® software calculations. A cold rolled sample showed high compressive yield strength of about 950 MPa, and the annealed sample had only half the strength of the cold rolled condition. The cold rolled sample shows the highest micro-hardness. The wear resistance of the annealed condition was significantly improved at room temperature and at 200 °C.
